We compare matched architectural instantiations of \emph{integrative encoding}, which compresses ambiguous evidence before a query is known, and \emph{retrieval-based inference}, which combines stored episodes after the query identifies the relevant causal relation. We introduce Consolidated Orthogonal LoRA Subspaces (COLORS), a continual learning framework that enables foundational models to learn an expanding set of tasks while consolidating shared skills, with minimal parameter growth and without forgetting previously learned tasks. Under a cheaply verifiable incoherence condition between tasks, we further show that each new task can be learned to near-oracle quality. Our approach addresses a growing challenge created by the widespread use of low-rank adapters (LoRAs): while LoRAs make it easy to adapt foundation models to individual tasks, they provide no principled mechanism for organizing or consolidating knowledge across tasks. Existing continual learning methods either repeatedly update a shared subspace, causing \textit{task drift}, or add new parameters for each new task, which increases model size and training costs as more tasks are learned.
